## Security

Fineract is **secure by design**. It is designed and built from the ground up to accept, manage, and present data securely. This chapter will detail its various security-related features and settings, along with best practices for secure deployment.

If you believe you have found a security vulnerability in Fineract itself, [let us know privately](https://fineract.apache.org/#contribute). Report security issues in third party code (for example, the [Mifos X Web UI](https://github.com/openMF/web-app)) to the appropriate third party, not Fineract.

Your task as bank CTO, sysadmin, vendor, or other entity responsible for hosting Fineract securely is to thoroughly consider these sections and thoughtfully apply them in your work. While a Fineract release *is* secure by design, it is *not* sufficient for a sysadmin to simply start it up and hope for the best. Careful steps must be taken to ensure a deployment is and remains secure despite software environment changes, attacks, staff transitions, and anything else that may arise.

We’ll first cover the various supported authentication schemes and will continue on to recommendations for securing a Fineract deployment.

> [!NOTE]
> The HTTP Basic and OAuth authentication schemes are mutually exclusive. You can’t enable them both at the same time. Fineract checks these settings on startup and will fail if more than one authentication scheme is enabled.

### HTTP Basic Authentication

By default Fineract is configured with a HTTP Basic Authentication scheme, so you actually don’t have to do anything if you want to use it. But if you would like to explicitly choose this authentication scheme then there are two ways to enable it:

1. Use environment variables (best choice if you run with Docker Compose):
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  FINERACT_SECURITY_BASICAUTH_ENABLED=true
  FINERACT_SECURITY_OAUTH_ENABLED=false
  ```
2. Use JVM parameters (best choice if you run the Spring Boot JAR):
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  java -Dfineract.security.basicauth.enabled=true -Dfineract.security.oauth2.enabled=false -jar fineract-provider.jar
  ```

### OAuth

Fineract has basic OAuth support based on Spring Boot Security.

This can be enabled at runtime in one of two ways:

1. Use environment variables (best choice if you run with Docker Compose):
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  FINERACT_SECURITY_BASICAUTH_ENABLED=false
  FINERACT_SECURITY_OAUTH_ENABLED=true
  FINERACT_SERVER_OAUTH_RESOURCE_URL=http://localhost:9000/realms/fineract
  ```
2. Use JVM parameters (best choice if you run the Spring Boot JAR):
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  java -Dfineract.security.basicauth.enabled=false -Dfineract.security.oauth2.enabled=true -jar fineract-provider.jar
  ```

Here’s how to test OAuth with [Keycloak](https://www.keycloak.org).
The steps required for other OAuth providers will be similar.

#### Set up Keycloak

1. From terminal, run: `docker run -p 9000:8080 -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.2.5 start-dev`
2. Go to URL 'http://localhost:9000/admin' and login with admin/admin
3. Click 'Manage realms', then 'Create realm'
4. Enter name `fineract` for the realm name
5. Click on tab 'Users' on the left, then 'Create new user' with username `mifos`, email `test@example.com`, First name `Mifos`, Last name `User`
6. Click on tab 'Credentials' at the top, and set password to `password`, turning 'temporary' setting to off
7. Click on tab 'Clients' on the left, and create client with ID `community-app`
8. In Settings tab, set 'Valid redirect URIs' to `localhost`, enable 'Client authentication', check 'Direct access grants'
9. Click 'Save' and a 'Credentials' tab will appear
10. In Credentials tab, copy string in field 'secret' as this will be needed in the step to request the access token

Finally we need to change Keycloak configuration so that it uses the username as a subject of the token:

1. Choose client `community-app` in the tab 'Clients'
2. Click on tab 'Client scopes', then `community-app-dedicated`
3. Go to tab 'Mappers', click 'Configure a new mapper' and choose 'User Property'
4. Enter `usernameInSub` as 'Name'
5. Enter `username` into the field 'Property' and `sub` into the field 'Token Claim Name'

You are now ready to test out OAuth:

#### Retrieve an access token from Keycloak

```bash
curl --request POST \
  "$FINERACT_SERVER_OAUTH_RESOURCE_URL/protocol/openid-connect/token" \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data-urlencode 'username=mifos' \
  --data-urlencode 'password=password' \
  --data-urlencode 'client_id=community-app' \
  --data-urlencode 'grant_type=password' \
  --data-urlencode 'client_secret=<enter the client secret from credentials tab>'
```

The reply should contain a field `access_token`. Copy the field’s value and use it in the API call below:

#### Invoke APIs and passAuthorization: bearer …​header

```bash
curl --insecure \
  'https://localhost:8443/fineract-provider/api/v1/offices' \
  --header 'Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default' \
  --header 'Authorization: bearer <enter the value of the access_token field>'
```

> [!NOTE]
> See also [fineract.apache.org/docs/legacy/#authentication_oauth](https://fineract.apache.org/docs/legacy/#authentication_oauth)

### Two-factor authentication

You can enable 2FA authentication. Depending on how you start Fineract add the following:

1. Use environment variables (best choice if you run with Docker Compose):
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  FINERACT_SECURITY_2FA_ENABLED=true
  ```
2. Use JVM parameter (best choice if you run the Spring Boot JAR):
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  java -Dfineract.security.2fa.enabled=true -jar fineract-provider.jar
  ```

### OIDC Federation

OIDC Federation allows Apache Fineract to delegate authentication to an external Identity Provider (IdP) â Keycloak, Azure Active Directory, Okta, Auth0, Google, or any standards-compliant OpenID Connect server â while keeping its existing multi-tenant user model intact.

When enabled, Fineract accepts signed JWTs issued by the configured IdP as Bearer tokens on all `/api/**` requests, resolving the incoming identity to a Fineract `AppUser` before the request reaches any business logic.

#### Architecture Overview

![OIDC Federation Architecture â Multi-Tenant](data:image/png;base64,)

The key design principle is **one IdP per tenant**: each Fineract tenant has its own IdP record in the master database, keyed by the JWT `iss` claim. A single Fineract instance can serve multiple tenants, each authenticating against a completely different IdP (Keycloak, Google, Azure AD, etc.) without any server restart.

```java
Tenant A (Keycloak) âââº JWT  âââ
Tenant B (Google)   âââº JWT  âââ¤âââº OidcTenantAwareFilter
Tenant C (Azure AD) âââº JWT  âââ         â
                                          â¼
                              DynamicJwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver
                                  â  reads JWT 'iss' claim
                                  âââ Priority 1: m_tenant_oidc_config (Master DB)
                                  â     â CRUD via REST API, no restart required
                                  âââ Priority 2: issuers[] (YAML, dev/CI fallback)
                                          â  builds + caches AuthenticationManager
                                          â¼
                              FineractOidcJwtAuthenticationConverter
                                  â  maps JWT â AppUser (username / email / auto-create)
                                  â¼
                              Business Logic (AppUser principal â same as Basic Auth)
```

Downstream Fineract services receive a standard `AppUser` principal with no code changes required.

#### Provider-Specific Setup Guides

* [Google Identity Provider â step-by-step](https://fineract.apache.org/docs/oidc-federation-google.html)

#### Prerequisites

* Fineract 1.x (Spring Boot 3)
* An IdP reachable from the Fineract server
* The IdP’s issuer URI (for OIDC discovery) or JWK Set URI

#### Issuer Resolution Priority

`DynamicJwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver` routes each incoming JWT to the correct IdP validator using the following priority chain:

| Priority | Source |
| --- | --- |
| 1 (highest) | Per-tenant config stored in `m_tenant_oidc_config` master DB table (managed via the OIDC Config API). |
| 2 | Static `fineract.security.oidc-federation.issuers[]` list in `application.yml` â suitable for dev/CI environments where all tenants share the same IdP. |

If no match is found for the JWT’s `iss` claim, the request is rejected with HTTP 401 (`unknown_issuer`).

The resolved `AuthenticationManager` for each issuer URI is cached in memory and invalidated automatically when the DB config changes.

#### Configuration Properties

All global properties are under `fineract.security.oidc-federation.*`.

| Property | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `false` | Master switch. Set to `true` to activate the OIDC filter chain. |
| `tenant-claim-name` | `fineract_tenant` | JWT claim used to resolve the Fineract tenant ID. Falls back to the `Fineract-Platform-TenantId` header, then the `tenantIdentifier` query parameter. |
| `username-claim` | `preferred_username` | JWT claim used as the Fineract username. Common alternatives: `email`, `sub`. Can be overridden per-issuer in the `issuers[]` list or the DB config. |
| `auto-create-user` | `false` | When `true`, a Fineract `AppUser` is created automatically on the first successful login for an unknown identity. When `false`, login fails with HTTP 401 unless the user already exists. |
| `default-roles` | *(empty)* | Comma-separated Fineract role names assigned to auto-created users (e.g. `Read-Only Role,Branch Manager`). |
| `provider` | `generic` | Controls the RP-Initiated Logout URL format. Values: `keycloak`, `azure_ad`, `okta`, `auth0`, `google`, `generic`. |
| `post-logout-redirect-uri` | *(empty)* | URI sent to the IdP after logout. When blank, defaults to the request’s base URL + `/login?logout`. |
| `issuers[]` | *(empty)* | Static per-issuer configuration list (YAML fallback). See YAML Issuer List Fallback for details. |

#### YAML Issuer List Fallback

The `issuers[]` list provides static per-issuer configuration for environments where the DB-based API is not used (local development, CI). Each entry in the list defines a trusted issuer and its JWT validation settings.

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      issuers:
        - issuerUri: https://keycloak.example.com/realms/fineract   (1)
          tenantId: default                                          (2)
          jwksUri: ""                                                (3)
          usernameClaim: preferred_username                          (4)
        - issuerUri: https://accounts.google.com
          tenantId: google-tenant
          usernameClaim: email
```

| **1** | Exact value of the JWT `iss` claim. Must match exactly, including trailing slashes. |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Fineract tenant identifier this issuer maps to. Used for tenant resolution when no JWT claim or header is present. |
| **3** | Optional. If blank or absent, the JWK Set URI is derived automatically from `issuerUri` via OIDC discovery (fetches `{issuerUri}/.well-known/openid-configuration`). |
| **4** | Optional per-issuer override for the username claim. Falls back to the global `username-claim` property if absent. |

> [!NOTE]
> The `issuers[]` list is a development/CI convenience. For production multi-tenant deployments, configure IdPs via the OIDC Config API so that each tenant’s settings are stored in the master database and can be updated without a server restart.

#### Per-Tenant OIDC Configuration API

Each Fineract tenant can be independently linked to a different IdP. The configuration is stored in the `m_tenant_oidc_config` master database table and is consulted at runtime by `DynamicJwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver` on every authenticated request. Changes take effect immediately â no server restart is required.

All endpoints require the `MANAGE_TENANT_OIDC_CONFIG` permission (Super Admin only). The `clientSecret` is accepted on write operations but is **never** returned in responses â it is stored AES-256-GCM encrypted.

##### Multi-Tenant Setup Example

The following example configures three tenants, each using a different IdP, against a running Fineract instance. All calls use Basic Auth from the admin tenant (`default`).

###### Tenant A â Keycloak

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-a/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "KEYCLOAK",
    "issuerUri": "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/tenant-a",        (1)
    "clientId": "fineract-tenant-a",
    "clientSecret": "keycloak-secret-a",
    "jwksUri": "",                                                       (2)
    "usernameClaim": "preferred_username",
    "scopes": "openid,profile,email",
    "postLogoutRedirectUri": "https://app.example.com/tenant-a/login?logout",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

| **1** | Each realm in Keycloak has a distinct issuer URI. This is the JWT `iss` value Fineract will match. |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Empty string â Fineract derives the JWK Set URI automatically from `issuerUri + /.well-known/openid-configuration`. |

Expected response:

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "tenantId": "tenant-a",
  "providerType": "KEYCLOAK",
  "issuerUri": "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/tenant-a",
  "clientId": "fineract-tenant-a",
  "usernameClaim": "preferred_username",
  "scopes": "openid,profile,email",
  "postLogoutRedirectUri": "https://app.example.com/tenant-a/login?logout",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Note that `clientSecret` is **absent** from the response â it is stored encrypted and never returned.

###### Tenant B â Google

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-b/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "GOOGLE",
    "issuerUri": "https://accounts.google.com",                          (1)
    "clientId": "123456789-xxxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com",
    "clientSecret": "GOCSPX-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "jwksUri": "https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs",            (2)
    "usernameClaim": "email",                                            (3)
    "scopes": "openid,email,profile",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

| **1** | Google’s issuer URI is always `accounts.google.com` regardless of the project. |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Optional â explicitly set here to avoid an OIDC discovery round-trip on first use. |
| **3** | Google ID tokens expose the user’s identity via the `email` claim. |

###### Tenant C â Azure Active Directory

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-c/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "AZURE_AD",
    "issuerUri": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/YOUR_TENANT_ID/v2.0",  (1)
    "clientId": "your-azure-app-client-id",
    "clientSecret": "your-azure-app-secret",
    "jwksUri": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/YOUR_TENANT_ID/discovery/v2.0/keys",
    "usernameClaim": "preferred_username",
    "scopes": "openid,profile,email",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

| **1** | Replace `YOUR_TENANT_ID` with the Azure AD Directory (tenant) ID from the App Registration overview. |
| --- | --- |

###### Verify All Three Are Registered

```bash
# Tenant A
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-a/oidc-config \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" | jq '{tenantId,providerType,issuerUri,enabled}'

# Tenant B
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-b/oidc-config \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" | jq '{tenantId,providerType,issuerUri,enabled}'

# Tenant C
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-c/oidc-config \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" | jq '{tenantId,providerType,issuerUri,enabled}'
```

##### Using Each Tenant’s IdP

Once registered, each tenant’s users authenticate by passing a JWT from their respective IdP. Fineract reads the `iss` claim to route the token to the correct validator automatically â the client only needs to pass its own IdP’s token.

```bash
# Tenant A user â token from Keycloak
KEYCLOAK_TOKEN="eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/clients \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${KEYCLOAK_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: tenant-a"

# Tenant B user â token from Google
GOOGLE_TOKEN="eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjZmNzI1N..."
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/clients \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${GOOGLE_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: tenant-b"

# Tenant C user â token from Azure AD
AZURE_TOKEN="eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsIng1..."
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/clients \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${AZURE_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: tenant-c"
```

> [!NOTE]
> The `Fineract-Platform-TenantId` header is the tenant resolution fallback used here because none of these standard tokens include a `fineract_tenant` claim. If your IdP injects a custom `fineract_tenant` claim into the JWT, the header is not needed.

##### Update Configuration

Update specific fields without touching the rest. On `PUT`, any field omitted from the request body retains its current database value.

```bash
# Disable Tenant B's Google IdP temporarily (e.g., during a credential rotation)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-b/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{ "enabled": false }'

# Rotate the client secret (omitting clientSecret on PUT preserves the existing encrypted value)
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-a/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{ "clientSecret": "new-rotated-secret" }'

# Migrate Tenant C from Azure AD to Okta
curl -X PUT http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-c/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "OKTA",
    "issuerUri": "https://dev-xxx.okta.com/oauth2/default",
    "clientId": "new-okta-client-id",
    "clientSecret": "new-okta-secret",
    "jwksUri": "",
    "usernameClaim": "preferred_username"
  }'
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> When updating `issuerUri`, the old issuer’s `AuthenticationManager` cache entry is evicted automatically. The new issuer is registered on the next authenticated request â no restart needed.

##### Delete Configuration

```bash
# Remove the OIDC config for Tenant B (fallback to Basic Auth or other auth mechanism)
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/tenant-b/oidc-config \
  -H "Authorization: Basic $(echo -n 'mifos:password' | base64)" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default"
```

After deletion, the in-memory `AuthenticationManager` cache entry for that issuer URI is evicted immediately. Subsequent requests carrying a JWT from the deleted issuer are rejected with HTTP 401 (`unknown_issuer`) â no server restart required.

##### Configuration Fields

| Field | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `providerType` | Yes | `KEYCLOAK`, `GOOGLE`, `AZURE_AD`, `OKTA`, `AUTH0`, or `GENERIC`. |
| `issuerUri` | Yes | Exact value of the JWT `iss` claim. Must be globally unique across all tenants. |
| `clientId` | Yes | OAuth2 Client ID registered with the IdP. |
| `clientSecret` | No | OAuth2 Client Secret. Encrypted at rest. Never returned in responses. |
| `jwksUri` | No | JWK Set URI for JWT signature verification. Derived from `issuerUri` via OIDC discovery if absent. |
| `usernameClaim` | No (default: `preferred_username`) | JWT claim used as the Fineract username. |
| `scopes` | No (default: `openid,profile,email`) | Comma-separated OAuth2 scopes. |
| `postLogoutRedirectUri` | No | URI sent to the IdP after logout. |
| `enabled` | No (default: `true`) | Set to `false` to disable this IdP without deleting the configuration. |

##### Database Schema

The `m_tenant_oidc_config` table lives in the master (tenant-store) database and is created by a Liquibase migration on startup.

```sql
CREATE TABLE m_tenant_oidc_config (
    id                    BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id             VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,  -- matches tenants.identifier
    provider_type         VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL,         -- KEYCLOAK | GOOGLE | AZURE_AD | OKTA | AUTH0 | GENERIC
    issuer_uri            VARCHAR(500)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,  -- JWT 'iss' claim, resolution key
    client_id             VARCHAR(255)  NOT NULL,
    client_secret         VARCHAR(1000),                  -- AES-256-GCM encrypted
    jwks_uri              VARCHAR(500),                   -- derived from issuer_uri if absent
    username_claim        VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'preferred_username',
    scopes                VARCHAR(500)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'openid,profile,email',
    post_logout_redirect_uri VARCHAR(500),
    enabled               TINYINT(1)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_at            DATETIME(6)  NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
    updated_at            DATETIME(6)  NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6)
);
```

#### Quick Start: Keycloak

##### Option A â Database (Recommended for Production)

1. Start Fineract with OIDC enabled:
  
  
  
  
  ```yaml
  fineract:
    security:
      oidc-federation:
        enabled: true
        auto-create-user: false
        username-claim: preferred_username
  ```
2. Register the Keycloak IdP via the API:
  
  
  
  
  ```bash
  curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/default/oidc-config \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "Authorization: Basic <admin-credentials>" \
    -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
    -d '{
      "providerType": "KEYCLOAK",
      "issuerUri": "https://keycloak.example.com/realms/fineract",
      "clientId": "fineract-app",
      "clientSecret": "s3cr3t",
      "usernameClaim": "preferred_username",
      "enabled": true
    }'
  ```
3. In Keycloak, add a client scope with a mapper of type **User Attribute** that injects the Fineract tenant identifier into the `fineract_tenant` claim.

##### Option B â YAML (Development/CI)

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      provider: keycloak
      auto-create-user: false
      issuers:
        - issuerUri: https://keycloak.example.com/realms/fineract
          tenantId: default
          usernameClaim: preferred_username
```

#### Quick Start: Azure Active Directory

##### Option A â Database

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/default/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic <admin-credentials>" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "AZURE_AD",
    "issuerUri": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/v2.0",
    "clientId": "your-app-client-id",
    "clientSecret": "your-app-secret",
    "jwksUri": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/discovery/v2.0/keys",
    "usernameClaim": "preferred_username",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

##### Option B â YAML

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      provider: azure_ad
      issuers:
        - issuerUri: https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/v2.0
          tenantId: default
          jwksUri: https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant-id}/discovery/v2.0/keys
          usernameClaim: preferred_username
```

Add an optional claims configuration in your Azure App Registration to include `preferred_username` in access tokens. Add `fineract_tenant` as a custom optional claim pointing to an extension attribute or app role.

#### Quick Start: Okta

##### Option A â Database

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/default/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic <admin-credentials>" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "OKTA",
    "issuerUri": "https://dev-xxx.okta.com/oauth2/default",
    "clientId": "your-okta-client-id",
    "clientSecret": "your-okta-secret",
    "usernameClaim": "preferred_username",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

##### Option B â YAML

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      provider: okta
      issuers:
        - issuerUri: https://dev-xxx.okta.com/oauth2/default
          tenantId: default
          usernameClaim: preferred_username
```

Use Okta’s **Groups claims** or a custom attribute in the Okta Expression Language to populate `fineract_tenant`.

#### Quick Start: Auth0

##### Option A â Database

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/default/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic <admin-credentials>" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "AUTH0",
    "issuerUri": "https://your-tenant.us.auth0.com/",
    "clientId": "your-auth0-client-id",
    "clientSecret": "your-auth0-secret",
    "usernameClaim": "nickname",
    "postLogoutRedirectUri": "https://your-fineract-app.example.com/login?logout",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

##### Option B â YAML

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      provider: auth0
      tenant-claim-name: https://fineract.apache.org/tenant
      issuers:
        - issuerUri: https://your-tenant.us.auth0.com/
          tenantId: default
          usernameClaim: nickname
```

Auth0 namespaces custom claims with a URI prefix. Use an Auth0 Action to add `fineract.apache.org/tenant` to the access token.

#### Tenant Resolution

`OidcTenantAwareFilter` resolves the active tenant in priority order:

1. Configurable JWT claim (value of `tenant-claim-name` property)
2. HTTP header `Fineract-Platform-TenantId`
3. Query parameter `tenantIdentifier`

If no tenant can be resolved, the filter chain continues without setting a tenant context; subsequent Spring Security validation will reject the request.

#### User Resolution

On every authenticated request, `FineractOidcJwtAuthenticationConverter` maps the incoming JWT to a Fineract `AppUser`:

1. Look up by username (value of the `username-claim` claim, or the per-issuer override from the DB config / `issuers[]` entry).
2. Fall back to email lookup if the username is not found.
3. If still not found and `auto-create-user=true`: create a new `AppUser` with a random placeholder password, assigned to the head office (id=1) and the roles listed in `default-roles`.
4. If not found and `auto-create-user=false`: reject with HTTP 401.

The resolved `AppUser` is set as the principal in a `FineractJwtAuthenticationToken`, ensuring full compatibility with all existing Fineract services without any code changes.

#### Running Alongside Basic Auth

Both authentication modes can be active simultaneously. The OIDC filter chain runs at `@Order(100)` and targets `/api/`. The Basic Auth chain has no explicit order (lowest priority). Requests to `/api/` with a `Bearer` token are handled by the OIDC chain; requests with an `Authorization: Basic` header fall through to the Basic Auth chain.

When both are enabled, a single `CorsConfigurationSource` bean is shared via `FineractCorsConfiguration`, preventing duplicate bean registration errors.

#### RP-Initiated Logout

Browser-based sessions can perform IdP logout via `GET /logout`. The redirect URL sent to the IdP depends on the `provider` property:

| Provider | Logout URL pattern |
| --- | --- |
| `keycloak` | `{issuer}/protocol/openid-connect/logout?id_token_hint={token}&post_logout_redirect_uri={uri}` |
| `azure_ad` | `{issuer}/oauth2/v2.0/logout?post_logout_redirect_uri={uri}` |
| `okta` | `{issuer}/v1/logout?id_token_hint={token}&post_logout_redirect_uri={uri}` |
| `auth0` | `{issuer}/v2/logout?returnTo={uri}` |
| `google` | Spring’s `OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler` uses Google’s discovered `end_session_endpoint` |
| `generic` | Spring’s `OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler` uses the IdP’s discovered `end_session_endpoint` |

RP-Initiated Logout only applies to the browser login redirect flow. Stateless Bearer token API clients do not use it.

#### Environment Variables

All properties can be overridden with environment variables, following Spring Boot’s relaxed binding rules:

```bash
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_FEDERATION_ENABLED=true
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_TENANT_CLAIM=fineract_tenant
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_USERNAME_CLAIM=preferred_username
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_AUTO_CREATE_USER=false
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_DEFAULT_ROLES=Read-Only Role
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_PROVIDER=keycloak
FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_POST_LOGOUT_URI=https://app.example.com/login?logout
```

The `issuers[]` list can only be configured via YAML. Use the OIDC Config API for dynamic, restart-free configuration.

#### Verification Checklist

After configuring OIDC, verify the following scenarios:

##### 1. Tenant resolution fallback chain

```bash
# Via JWT claim (configure IdP to include fineract_tenant claim)
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt-with-tenant-claim>" https://fineract/api/v1/clients

# Via header
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt>" \
     -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
     https://fineract/api/v1/clients

# Via query param
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <jwt>" \
     "https://fineract/api/v1/clients?tenantIdentifier=default"
```

##### 2. Issuer resolution (multi-IdP)

Send tokens from two different IdPs and confirm each resolves to the correct tenant and user.

##### 3. Principal compatibility

After a successful request, confirm that `SpringSecurityPlatformSecurityContext.authenticatedUser()` returns the expected `AppUser` with no `ClassCastException`. Any Fineract endpoint that accesses the current user (e.g., `GET /api/v1/users/me`) exercises this path.

##### 4. Auto-create disabled (default)

Send a valid IdP token for a username that does not exist in Fineract. Expect HTTP 401 with an error body referencing `auto-create-user`.

##### 5. Auto-create enabled

With `auto-create-user=true`, send a valid token for a new user. Confirm:

* HTTP 200 on the first request.
* A new row appears in `m_appuser` with the expected username.
* Subsequent requests resolve the same `AppUser`.

##### 6. No duplicate bean errors

Enable both `fineract.security.basicauth.enabled=true` and `fineract.security.oidc-federation.enabled=true`. Confirm:

* Exactly one `CorsConfigurationSource` bean in the context.
* No `BeanDefinitionStoreException` on startup.
* No duplicate `@EnableMethodSecurity` error.

##### 7. RP-Initiated Logout redirect

With a browser session, navigate to `GET /logout`. Confirm the browser is redirected to the IdP’s end-session endpoint with the correct URL structure for your configured provider.

##### 8. Unknown issuer rejection

Send a JWT whose `iss` claim does not match any DB config or YAML `issuers[]` entry. Expect HTTP 401 with `unknown_issuer`.

##### 9. DB config cache invalidation

After calling `DELETE /api/v1/tenants/{tenantId}/oidc-config`, confirm that subsequent requests from the deleted issuer are rejected with HTTP 401 without a server restart.

#### Troubleshooting

**HTTP 401 â "No Fineract user found for OIDC subject"**

The `preferred_username` (or configured `username-claim`) in the token does not match any Fineract user. Either create the user in Fineract, enable `auto-create-user=true`, or change `username-claim` to match how your users are named in Fineract.

**HTTP 401 â "unknown_issuer"**

The JWT `iss` claim does not match any entry in `m_tenant_oidc_config` or the `issuers[]` YAML list. Register the issuer via the OIDC Config API or add it to the `issuers[]` list.

**HTTP 401 â JWT signature verification failed**

The `issuerUri` or `jwksUri` is incorrect, or the IdP’s JWK Set is not reachable from the Fineract server. Check network connectivity and the configured URIs.

**Tenant context not set (NullPointerException on tenant)**

The token does not include the configured `tenant-claim-name` claim, the `Fineract-Platform-TenantId` header is missing, and the `tenantIdentifier` query parameter is absent. Configure the IdP to include the tenant claim, or always pass the header.

**Startup failure: "No qualifying bean of type CorsConfigurationSource"**

Ensure `fineract-provider` is on the classpath. The shared `FineractCorsConfiguration` bean lives there.

**OIDC Config API returns 403**

The authenticated user does not have the `MANAGE_TENANT_OIDC_CONFIG` permission. Assign this permission to the Super Admin role.

### OIDC Federation â Google Identity Provider

This guide walks through configuring Google as an OIDC Identity Provider for Apache Fineract step by step, from creating a Google Cloud project to sending authenticated API requests.

#### Prerequisites

* A Google account with access to [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com)
* A running Fineract instance (local or remote)
* `curl` and `jq` installed locally

> [!NOTE]
> Google’s standard ID tokens do **not** include a `fineract_tenant` claim. The tenant is resolved either from the `tenantId` field in the OIDC config (DB or YAML `issuers[]` entry), from the `Fineract-Platform-TenantId` HTTP header, or from the `tenantIdentifier` query parameter. This is normal and safe for development; in production you would add a custom claim via a Google Workspace domain-wide policy or a middleware token enricher.

#### Step 1: Create a Google Cloud Project

1. Go to [console.cloud.google.com](https://console.cloud.google.com).
2. Click the project selector in the top bar â **New Project**.
3. Enter a name such as `fineract-oidc-test` and click **Create**.
4. Wait for the project to be created (a few seconds), then select it from the project selector.

#### Step 2: Configure the OAuth Consent Screen

The OAuth consent screen is shown to users when they authorize your application. It must be configured before creating credentials.

1. In the left navigation, go to **APIs & Services** â **OAuth consent screen**.
2. Under "User Type", select:
  
  
  
  
  
  * **Internal** â if you are using a Google Workspace account and only want users from your organization to log in (recommended for testing in a corporate environment).
  * **External** â if you are testing with personal Gmail accounts.
3. Click **Create**.
4. Fill in the required fields:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| App name | `Fineract OIDC Test` |
| User support email | your Google account email |
| Developer contact email | your Google account email |

1. Click **Save and Continue**.
2. On the **Scopes** step, click **Add or Remove Scopes** and add:
  
  
  
  
  ```java
  openid
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.email
  https://www.googleapis.com/auth/userinfo.profile
  ```
  
  
  
  
  
  Click **Update**, then **Save and Continue**.
3. On the **Test users** step (only for External apps), click **Add Users** and enter your Gmail address. Click **Save and Continue**.
4. Review the summary and click **Back to Dashboard**.

#### Step 3: Create OAuth 2.0 Credentials

1. In **APIs & Services** â **Credentials**, click **Create Credentials** â **OAuth client ID**.
2. Under **Application type**, select **Web application**.
3. Enter a name: `Fineract Local Test`.
4. Under **Authorized redirect URIs**, click **Add URI** and add:
  
  
  
  
  ```java
  http://localhost:8080/login/oauth2/code/google
  ```
  
  
  
  
  
  This URI is required for the browser login redirect flow. Add `developers.google.com/oauthplayground` as a second URI to enable token acquisition via the OAuth 2.0 Playground (used in Step 5).
5. Click **Create**.
6. A dialog appears with your credentials. Note the two values â you will need them shortly:
  
  
  
  
  ```java
  Client ID:     xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com
  Client Secret: GOCSPX-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
  ```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Do not commit these values to version control. Use environment variables or a secrets manager.

#### Step 4: Understand the Google OIDC Endpoints

Google exposes all OIDC metadata via its discovery document. You can verify it at any time:

```bash
curl https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .
```

The key values for Fineract configuration are:

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Issuer URI | `accounts.google.com` |
| JWK Set URI | `www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs` |
| Authorization endpoint | `accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth` |
| Token endpoint | `oauth2.googleapis.com/token` |

#### Step 5: Configure Fineract

Fineract resolves IdP configurations using a priority chain: DB-stored config takes precedence over static YAML. Choose whichever option fits your environment.

##### Option A â Register Google via the API (Recommended)

Register Google as the IdP for the `default` tenant using the OIDC Config REST API. No server restart required; the in-memory cache updates immediately.

First, enable OIDC globally:

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      provider: google
      auto-create-user: true           (1)
      default-roles: ""
```

| **1** | Set to `true` for testing so Fineract auto-creates a user on the first login. For production, set to `false` and pre-create users. |
| --- | --- |

Then register the Google IdP via the REST API:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/tenants/default/oidc-config \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic <admin-credentials>" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "providerType": "GOOGLE",
    "issuerUri": "https://accounts.google.com",     (1)
    "clientId": "YOUR_CLIENT_ID",
    "clientSecret": "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET",
    "usernameClaim": "email",                       (2)
    "scopes": "openid,email,profile",
    "enabled": true
  }'
```

| **1** | Google’s OIDC discovery document is at `accounts.google.com/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Fineract fetches the JWK Set URI automatically from the discovery document. |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Google ID tokens include `email`. This maps the Google email to the Fineract username. |

##### Option B â YAML Issuer List (Development/CI)

Use the `issuers[]` property for a fully static configuration without database interaction.

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      provider: google                      (1)
      auto-create-user: true
      issuers:
        - issuerUri: https://accounts.google.com   (2)
          tenantId: default                        (3)
          usernameClaim: email                     (4)
```

| **1** | Use the `google` provider type. Logout delegates to Spring’s `OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler`, which discovers Google’s `end_session_endpoint` automatically. |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | Google’s issuer URI. The JWK Set URI is derived automatically via OIDC discovery. |
| **3** | Fineract tenant identifier for tokens from this issuer. Google does not include a `fineract_tenant` claim, so the `tenantId` here acts as the fallback mapping. |
| **4** | Google ID tokens include `email`. Overrides the global `username-claim` for this issuer. |

Equivalent environment variable overrides for Option B global settings:

```bash
export FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_FEDERATION_ENABLED=true
export FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_PROVIDER=google
export FINERACT_SECURITY_OIDC_AUTO_CREATE_USER=true
```

> [!NOTE]
> Google’s standard ID tokens do **not** include a `fineract_tenant` claim. The tenant is resolved from the `tenantId` mapping in the `issuers[]` entry (Option B) or from the `m_tenant_oidc_config` record (Option A). When calling the API directly without a browser session, you can also pass `Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default` as a header.

##### 5.2 Audience Validation (Recommended for Production)

Google issues ID tokens with an `aud` claim set to your Client ID. By default, Spring Security’s resource server does not validate the audience, which means any Google ID token from any application would be accepted.

For production environments, configure audience validation by adding a `SecurityFilterChain` customizer or by subclassing `OidcFederationSecurityConfig`. A quick way using Spring Boot auto-configuration:

```yaml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://accounts.google.com
          # Audience validation (Spring Boot 3.x)
          # Set to your OAuth2 Client ID to reject tokens from other apps:
          # audiences: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com
```

> [!NOTE]
> The `audiences` property under `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt` requires Spring Boot 3.3+. On earlier versions, configure it programmatically via `JwtDecoderFactory`.

##### 5.3 Optional: Browser Login Redirect Flow

Add these properties only if you want browser-based login (the OAuth2 authorization code redirect flow). This is separate from Bearer token API validation and is not required for API testing.

```yaml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          google:
            client-id: YOUR_CLIENT_ID
            client-secret: YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
            scope:
              - openid
              - email
              - profile
            redirect-uri: "{baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}"
        provider:
          google:
            issuer-uri: https://accounts.google.com
```

Replace `YOUR_CLIENT_ID` and `YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET` with the values from Step 3.

#### Step 6: Create a Fineract Test User (Manual Pre-Provisioning)

If `auto-create-user=false`, you must create the Fineract user before logging in. The username must match the `email` claim value from your Google account (since `usernameClaim: email` was configured in Step 5).

```bash
# Replace BASIC_AUTH_TOKEN with your current admin credentials (base64 of user:password)
# Replace your.email@gmail.com with the Gmail address you will use to log in

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Basic BASIC_AUTH_TOKEN" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -d '{
    "username": "your.email@gmail.com",
    "firstname": "Your",
    "lastname": "Name",
    "email": "your.email@gmail.com",
    "officeId": 1,
    "roles": [1],
    "sendPasswordToEmail": false,
    "password": "Change1t!",
    "repeatPassword": "Change1t!"
  }'
```

> [!TIP]
> If `auto-create-user=true`, skip this step. Fineract will create the `AppUser` automatically on the first successful Google login.

#### Step 7: Obtain a Google ID Token

Google issues two tokens: an **access token** (opaque, for Google APIs) and an **ID token** (a signed JWT, suitable as a Fineract Bearer token). Fineract validates the ID token.

##### Method A: OAuth2 Playground (Easiest â Recommended for Development)

1. Open [developers.google.com/oauthplayground](https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground).
2. Click the gear icon (â) in the top-right corner and enable:
  
  
  
  
  ```java
  â Use your own OAuth credentials
  ```
  
  
  
  
  
  Enter your Client ID and Client Secret from Step 3.
3. In the left panel under "Select & authorize APIs", scroll to the bottom and find **Step 1**. In the input box, enter:
  
  
  
  
  ```java
  openid email profile
  ```
  
  
  
  
  
  Click **Authorize APIs**. A Google consent screen appears â sign in with the account you will use for testing.
4. After authorization, you are redirected back to the Playground at **Step 2**. Click **Exchange authorization code for tokens**.
5. In the response panel, copy the value of `id_token`. This is a JWT signed by Google that Fineract will validate.

```json
{
  "access_token": "ya29.xxxxxxxx",
  "id_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6...",   <-- Copy this
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3599
}
```

> [!NOTE]
> ID tokens expire after 1 hour. If the token expires during testing, repeat Step 7 to obtain a new one.

##### Method B: Authorization Code Flow via cURL

This method is more suitable for scripted testing. It requires a browser for the initial authorization step.

```bash
# Step 1 â Build the authorization URL and open it in a browser
CLIENT_ID="YOUR_CLIENT_ID"
REDIRECT_URI="http://localhost:8080/login/oauth2/code/google"
SCOPE="openid%20email%20profile"
STATE="fineract-test"

AUTH_URL="https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth\
?client_id=${CLIENT_ID}\
&redirect_uri=${REDIRECT_URI}\
&response_type=code\
&scope=${SCOPE}\
&state=${STATE}\
&access_type=offline"

echo "Open this URL in your browser:"
echo "$AUTH_URL"
```

After authorizing, Google redirects to your `redirect_uri` with a `code` parameter in the URL. Copy the code value.

```bash
# Step 2 â Exchange the authorization code for tokens
CLIENT_SECRET="YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET"
CODE="4/xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"  # paste the code from the redirect URL

curl -s -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "code=${CODE}" \
  -d "client_id=${CLIENT_ID}" \
  -d "client_secret=${CLIENT_SECRET}" \
  -d "redirect_uri=${REDIRECT_URI}" \
  -d "grant_type=authorization_code" | jq .

# The response contains id_token â save it:
ID_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "code=${CODE}" \
  -d "client_id=${CLIENT_ID}" \
  -d "client_secret=${CLIENT_SECRET}" \
  -d "redirect_uri=${REDIRECT_URI}" \
  -d "grant_type=authorization_code" | jq -r '.id_token')

echo "ID Token: $ID_TOKEN"
```

##### Inspect the Token (Optional)

Before testing, you can inspect the token’s claims:

```bash
# Decode the JWT payload (no signature verification â for inspection only)
echo "$ID_TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .
```

Expected output (example):

```json
{
  "iss": "https://accounts.google.com",
  "azp": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com",
  "aud": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com",
  "sub": "117349871234567890123",
  "email": "yourname@gmail.com",
  "email_verified": true,
  "name": "Your Name",
  "given_name": "Your",
  "family_name": "Name",
  "iat": 1715000000,
  "exp": 1715003600
}
```

Notice there is no `fineract_tenant` claim. The tenant will be provided via the HTTP header in Step 8.

#### Step 8: Test the API with the Google ID Token

##### 8.1 Authenticated API Call

Use the `id_token` as a Bearer token and pass the Fineract tenant via the `Fineract-Platform-TenantId` header:

```bash
ID_TOKEN="eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs..."   # paste your id_token here

curl -v http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/users \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ID_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

Expected result for a successful authentication:

* HTTP 200 with a JSON list of Fineract users.
* A new row in `m_appuser` with `username = yourname@gmail.com` (if `auto-create-user=true`).

##### 8.2 Verify User Was Created (if auto-create is enabled)

```bash
# Query the database (replace with your MariaDB/PostgreSQL connection details)
mysql -u root -p fineract_default -e \
  "SELECT id, username, email, firstname, lastname, is_deleted \
   FROM m_appuser \
   WHERE username = 'yourname@gmail.com';"
```

##### 8.3 Confirm the AppUser Principal (principal casting test)

The following Fineract endpoint returns the currently authenticated user. If the OIDC principal is correctly set to `AppUser`, this call will succeed without a `ClassCastException`:

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/users/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ID_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default" \
  -H "Accept: application/json"
```

##### 8.4 Verify Rejection When Token is Absent or Invalid

```bash
# No token â expect 401
curl -I http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/users \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default"

# Tampered token â expect 401
curl -I http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/users \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInRhbXBlcmVkIjoidHJ1ZSJ9.INVALID.signature" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default"
```

##### 8.5 Verify Tenant Fallback Chain

Test each source in the resolution chain independently to confirm all three work:

```bash
# 1. Header (standard fallback when no JWT tenant claim)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/offices \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ID_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default"
# Expected: 200

# 2. Query parameter
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  "http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/offices?tenantIdentifier=default" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ID_TOKEN}"
# Expected: 200

# 3. No tenant at all
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
  http://localhost:8080/fineract-provider/api/v1/offices \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ID_TOKEN}"
# Expected: 401 or 400 (no tenant context)
```

#### Step 9: Test the Browser Login Flow (Optional)

This step requires the Spring OAuth2 client properties from Step 5.3.

1. Start Fineract with the browser login configuration.
2. Open a browser and navigate to `localhost:8080/login`.
3. Click **"Login with Google"** (or the equivalent button rendered by Spring Security’s default login page).
4. Complete the Google sign-in flow.
5. On success, you are redirected back to Fineract. Verify the Fineract logs show (DEBUG level):
  
  
  
  
  ```java
  DEBUG OidcAuthenticationSuccessHandler - OIDC login successful â user: 'yourname@gmail.com', tenant: 'default', Fineract id: 42
  ```
6. To test RP-Initiated Logout, navigate to `localhost:8080/logout`. With `provider: generic`, Spring uses Google’s discovered `end_session_endpoint` to end the Google session.

#### Step 10: Verify No Startup Conflicts (Both Auth Modes)

If Basic Auth is also enabled, confirm there are no bean conflicts:

```yaml
fineract:
  security:
    basicauth:
      enabled: true
    oidc-federation:
      enabled: true
      ...
```

```bash
# Start Fineract and check for these specific error patterns
grep -i "BeanDefinitionStoreException\|NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException\|EnableMethodSecurity" fineract.log
```

Expected: no matching lines. Exactly one `CorsConfigurationSource` bean should be registered (from `FineractCorsConfiguration`).

#### Fineract Logs Reference

When OIDC is working correctly, expect these log lines:

```java
# Converter extracting username from incoming JWT
DEBUG FineractOidcJwtAuthenticationConverter - Converting external IdP JWT for username 'yourname@gmail.com' (subject: '117349871234567890123')

# User resolved by username from the database
DEBUG OidcAppUserResolutionServiceImpl - OIDC user resolved by username: 'yourname@gmail.com'

# Tenant set from header fallback
DEBUG OidcTenantAwareFilter - OIDC tenant context set to 'default' for /fineract-provider/api/v1/users

# Auto-create (first login)
INFO  OidcAppUserResolutionServiceImpl - Auto-creating Fineract user for OIDC subject 'yourname@gmail.com'
INFO  OidcAppUserResolutionServiceImpl - Auto-created Fineract user 'yourname@gmail.com' (id=42) from OIDC identity
```

#### Troubleshooting

##### HTTP 401 â "OAuth2 Bearer token is invalid"

The JWT signature verification failed. Check:

* Is `spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri` set to exactly `accounts.google.com`?
* Is the network between Fineract and `www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs` open?
* Did you use the `id_token` (not the `access_token`) as the Bearer value?

Verify with:

```bash
# Fineract should be able to reach Google's JWK Set
curl https://www.googleapis.com/oauth2/v3/certs | jq .keys[0].kid
```

##### HTTP 401 â "No Fineract user found for OIDC subject"

The Google email address does not match any `m_appuser.username` in the database. Either:

* Enable `auto-create-user=true`, or
* Create the user manually (Step 6) with `username = yourname@gmail.com`.

##### HTTP 400 â "Required header 'Fineract-Platform-TenantId' is missing"

The Google token does not contain a `fineract_tenant` claim (expected â see the note at the top). Always pass `Fineract-Platform-TenantId: default` (or your tenant name) in the request header when using Google as the IdP.

##### Token Expired â HTTP 401

Google ID tokens are valid for 1 hour. Return to Step 7 and obtain a new token from the OAuth2 Playground.

##### "redirect_uri_mismatch" on Google Consent Screen

The `redirect_uri` in your request does not match what was configured in Step 3. Ensure `localhost:8080/login/oauth2/code/google` is listed as an authorized redirect URI in Google Cloud Console.

##### Consent Screen Shows "App not verified"

For External apps in testing mode, Google shows a warning. Click **Continue** â **Go to [App Name] (unsafe)**. This warning only appears for apps in testing mode with scopes that access user data.

#### Security Considerations for Production

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The following changes are **required** before using Google OIDC in a production environment.

1. **Disable `auto-create-user`**: Set `auto-create-user: false`. Pre-provision users via the Fineract Admin API and enforce role assignments through your provisioning workflow.
2. **Validate the audience**: Configure the JWT decoder to reject tokens not issued for your Client ID (see Step 5.2). This prevents tokens obtained by other Google apps from being accepted.
3. **Add a custom tenant claim**: Use a Google Workspace domain-wide policy or an API Gateway / OAuth2 Proxy to inject the `fineract_tenant` claim into tokens before they reach Fineract. This removes the dependency on the HTTP header for tenant resolution.
4. **Restrict scopes**: Request only `openid email profile`. Do not request Google Drive or other scopes.
5. **Rotate credentials**: Rotate the OAuth2 Client Secret regularly and store it in a secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, etc.), not in `application.yml`.
6. **Use HTTPS**: Ensure Fineract is served over HTTPS in production. Google will not issue tokens to non-HTTPS redirect URIs outside of `localhost`.
7. **Monitor failed logins**: `OidcUserNotFoundException` is logged at WARN level. Route these logs to your SIEM or alerting system to detect enumeration attempts.

### Securing Fineract

This section covers best practices in securing the use of Fineract.

Security hardening is a continuum and Fineract is adaptable to your security needs. There’s no one way to correctly deploy it and the open source project offers no warranty. It’s up to you to deploy and maintain it carefully, according to your organization’s needs and compliance requirements.

Since Fineract is a financial application with PII (personally identifiable information), it is vital that it is secured in production whenever it is setup. If you are a small financial entity, bank, credit union, microfinance organization, or non-banking financial institution, the project urges you to identify and work with the vendors that work regularly with Fineract and are regular contributors to the security fixes. In this way, we encourage a community of contributions that keep the overall solution secure. Open source gets the benefit of many people reviewing the code and suggesting issues and solutions - let’s ensure that virtuous cycle can work by supporting those working on security at Fineract.

Members of the Security team can be reached at security AT fineract.apache.org. The reporting mechanisms for vulnerabilities and exploits are there, not on the public dev list.

See apache security practices for more information. [security.apache.org](https://security.apache.org)

Also, we recommend you familiarize yourself with the OWASP foundation and the "Cheat Sheet" series [cheatsheetseries.owasp.org](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org)

#### Tips for securing the Fineract infrastructure

##### Pay attention to your logs

View, review, and continuously monitor your server logs. Heed `DO NOT USE THIS IN PRODUCTION!` warnings.

##### Do not enable Spring profiles

Spring profiles such as `test` must never be enabled in production environments. `test` enables insecure API endpoints only meant for dev/test.

See Kubernetes for a valid use of the `liquibase-only` Spring profile.

##### Run it isolated and/or disconnected

In the world of Microfinance or small banking operations (in some geographies), it is possible that you can run Fineract on a private network, or isolated from the internet by being hosted locally and securing all connections. This could involve establishing a VPN with limited ports open, and only accepting connections within that VPN. At the far end of this spectrum, is running it isolated and air-gapped as a backend accounting system, where there is no internet connection on that device. In such scenarios, you are limiting the vectors of attack to just those employees you give access to. You are also limiting the functionality to accounting and basic operations, so this is rarely appropriate.  Even in these scenarios, it is important that you establish reviews of logs and accounts on a periodic basis to determine if any internal fraud is occurring. Such things should be part of your operational manual. There are a number of resources available for this topic, please find them online. For Fineract in particular, be mindful of the set up of approvals and and the access you give to each person or role in your organization.

##### Running it connected but behind a firewall

It should be clear that running it on the internet directly, without API monitoring and filtering, is a bad idea. This is especially true if your Fineract instance is connected to a payment mechanism of any kind. Imagine an exploit being used to gain access and then to send funds from an account to an outside merchant or bank. An attacker could drain an account before you can detect the issue.  And, then it will depend on the payment scheme rules whether any of those funds are recoverable.

There are multiple ways to enhance the security that is built into Fineract, but none of them are bulletproof and so you must have defense in depth. One key thing is to run the Fineract instance behind an API gateway, and to prevent certain API patterns or calls that are likely to be fraudulent. The important thing is to recognize that while you may not be a target institution now, at any moment this can change, and your IP will be listed on the dark web as a potential target for exploit. Your IT team must also have ways to quickly turn off services to limit the damage.

It is recommended to run it with at least API Gateway, WAF (Web Application Firewall) and SQL Injection filtering tool if connecting to the internet. Fineract must be hardened to run in production.

##### Fraud prevention

Even if you have secured your infrastructure, you will need the ability to monitor fraudulent traffic, and then to stop that fraud in real time. Fraud can occur even when your infrastructure is good, but a user account has been accessed through a phishing attack or similar vector. And, in the world of real time payments and multiple payment types and channels, there is a need for additional real time monitoring, and inline processing of potential fraudulent transactions. Detection and blocking needs to occur in real time and then resolution can occur more leisurely with additional manual and help desk interventions.

If you are a small institution and you are getting into this situation, you should consider having holds on all payment and transfers built into your process, until you can enable effective tools.

There are a number of fraud prevention tools that are available in market from fraud prevention vendors. When looking for solution providers, the ideal scenario is a vendor with longevity and a track record in your market for detecting recent fraudulent activities. Pattern detection is a key part of this, and for that, it is important to be able to get enough data from your systems to identify the anomalies.

There are a number of GitHub projects that cover algorithms for conducting ML on transactions to detect anomalies. There is also an open source project, Tazama, which provides a kind of framework for your own logic and algorithms: [github.com/frmscoe/docs](https://github.com/frmscoe/docs).

Fraud exploits are on the rise, supercharged by AI tooling. AI tooling can also be used to fight these trends, but it is an ever escalating area of concern for financial providers globally.

##### Self-service APIs

It is recommended that you leave the Self Service APIs disabled to avoid any potential exploits there. Apps should not be developed to use those APIs.

There is a way to run those APIs endpoint (re-written but consistent) in a separate isolated component, where there is a way to control the ingress and egress of data. Once that component is linked up with authenticated users with a fully designed authorization scheme, then the APIs can be accessed.  This is an area of exploration by the project. Currently, Fineract should not be run in a way that allows access to those APIs. We strongly advise against using any APP that connects to those APIs without revising the architecture as described, except in a test or demo environment.

##### User Education and Training

Educating and training your team is another limb of your organizational cybersecurity defense. Equipped with engaging security awareness training sessions, end-users can be prepared with both knowledge and skills on how to identify potential security threats and react to them. You can get more information from some of the resources offered in the course during CISA Training: [www.cisa.gov](https://www.cisa.gov)

##### Regular Security Audits and Compliance Checks

Know your compliance surface. Regularly conduct routine security audits and compliance checks. This can be helpful in finding all the vulnerabilities and their fix prior to exploitation, thereby helping to reduce the exposure window. A combined automated tool with manual expert reviews provides complete coverage. There are multiple vendors available that scan for compliance with existing security standards. We don’t recommend any vendor in particular, but for pointers you can look at [owasp.org/www-community/Vulnerability_Scanning_Tools](https://owasp.org/www-community/Vulnerability_Scanning_Tools)

##### Key Management and Data Encryption Strategies

Implement strong data encryption strategies to protect sensitive information. Key management should be something that your IT team does, utilizing best practices. Just like a physical key, you should keep it in a secure location with limited access and take special care not to copy it to digital locations that can be scanned or found, including email systems. Make sure you have procedures in place.

You would probably want to encrypt the data at rest with AES-256 and in transit via TLS 1.3. Create and maintain binding standards for encryption in your organization. And remember, key management to encryption is the key. Every cloud providers provides key management services that help you manage and secure your keys.

Examples:

* [aws.amazon.com/kms/](https://aws.amazon.com/kms/)
* [cloud.google.com/docs/security/key-management-deep-dive](https://cloud.google.com/docs/security/key-management-deep-dive)
* [learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/key-management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/fundamentals/key-management)
* [github.com/getsops/sops](https://github.com/getsops/sops)
* [github.com/Infisical/infisical](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical)

##### Secure Coding Practices

Secure code by following secure coding practices and standards, such as OWASP’s top ten, for any kind of vulnerability at the code level. Use tools like SonarQube for finding security problems in your source code through static application security testing (SAST) prior to deploying an application. Note that SonarQube has already been integrated into our automation build process.

Apache Software Foundation has an account with SonarQube and Fineract scans can be found in that account.

##### Multi-factor Authentication (MFA)

Enhance your security layers with MFA (or 2FA: two-factor authentication). One such approach, built on three things: something the user knows (like a password), something the user has (like a security token), and something the user is (biometric verification, for example). When MFA is used, it adds another layer of security. Solutions such as Duo Security may be a good implementation for MFA.

##### Leverage Community Support

You should stay engaged with the Fineract community to stay on top of security updates, patches, and best practices. Also, look for the possibility of collaboration with cybersecurity firms that would help you increase the capability of your threat detection and response system. Such relationships may avail specialized skills, technologies, and intelligence that may strengthen the security posturing of your organization.
